utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may be seated. Good morning, ladies and gentlemen; good morning to the technical booth, the interpreters, legal assistants, court reporters, the registrar; good morning to the Office of the Prosecution, to Defence counsel, and the accused. We're going to resume our case. I think we are now due to continue with the cross-examination of the witness, but I have been informed that Mr. Keegan has something to tell us before we do that. So you have the floor, Mr. Keegan, bearing in mind that the witness is waiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I understand. And if I could request that we go into private session for this, please. It relates to witness protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We're going to go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness. Can you hear me well? You may be seated. I wish to remind you that you're still testifying under oath, and I think you're now going to be answering questions put to you by Mr. Fila. Excuse me, Mr. Fila. We're going to follow the order in the indictment, so I have to ask Mr. Nikolic first whether he wishes to cross-examine. But if you do wish to cross-examine, perhaps you can come after Mr. Fila, as Mr. Fila has already taken his place at the rostrum. If you agree. If not, we can change the order. Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. This Defence team, the Defence team for Milojica Kos, will not be cross-examining this witness and I'm saying this simply for the benefit of the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you for drawing my attention to this point, so we can proceed with Mr. Fila. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Mesanovic, I'm Toma Fila, an attorney from Belgrade, and together with Zoran Jovanovic, my colleague, I represent Mr. Krkan. I have a few brief questions for you, and I would like to ask you to give me brief answers. During your stay in the "white house," apart from Hajra, did you see any other woman detained there? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Who?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Jadranka. I don't know her surname.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So there were two women?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She was in the room in the middle, opposite the entrance, together with Lujo, I don't know his surname. A room in the middle.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, this was not a separate room where women were held, but you saw one with this Serb man, Drago -- no, never mind. I don't know the surname.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So one woman was in one room, and the other woman in another room?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: At the end of the corridor in the "white house," was there a small room without any door?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What was inside?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Jadranka and Lujo.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So they were in that room?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: How large was that room?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very small. The width was the same as that of the corridor. The length -- I wasn't inside. So it was short. The width was that of the corridor and the length was short.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: It would be roughly the size of a bathroom, shall we say.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: At one point, you said that a bus arrived from Keraterm.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: How do you know that it came from Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By what the prisoners said, because there had been people in Omarska who had been in Keraterm before, and they had seen those same people. Dzevad Hadzibegovic that I pointed to on the photograph, he had been in Keraterm, and when the bus came, he said, "Those people are from Keraterm."

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So they came during the day. Can you tell us, was it in the morning, in the afternoon?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in the morning, before noon.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And they passed through this double row of guards. Please tell me, if you can remember, who formed those rows.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Were there any civilians?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What about military men?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The guards, the guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The guards from Omarska?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And these people ran through the gauntlet. Did they walk or run?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They ran.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And you were able to see that well?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What happened then with the people who entered the "white house," as far as you were able to see?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing. I couldn't see anything, what was happening in the "white house."

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did they come back out and go to some other rooms or did they go for interrogation?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They just went for lunch and returned to the "white house."

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And that's all that happened to them?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: On the photographs taken from a video clip, I saw that you were lying there.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Will you tell me, while you were in that "glass house," and we're now going on to the "glass house" period, were you standing, sitting, or lying down?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most often we sat there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And as you sat, were you able to see well through the restaurant outside?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because I was in the extreme right-hand corner of the "glass house." So I had a view of the "white house."

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Were you able to see the area between the white and the "red house"?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the pillar, not further than. I couldn't see the "red house" from that corner.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And at mealtime, the people passing did not obstruct your view?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, they did. They did obstruct my view.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You said there were three shifts and who the shift leaders were. When were the shifts?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From 7.00 a.m. until 7.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: How did the changeover take place?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They arrived by bus. They took their positions. I know that the same group of people came where we were. One group came, the other group left using the same bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did anyone distribute them or did they know in advance where their positions were?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I arrived on the 24th of June, so they probably knew from before where their positions were, because Ranko and the electrician, they always came to the "glass house." I remembered them best, because they were the worst, and they never had positions elsewhere while I was there, from the 24th of June until the 6th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I was inquiring about the procedure. You have some military experience. You have group leaders, squads, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that wasn't the classical military procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So it wasn't in the way it's done in the army.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I think not. I didn't see a leader leading the group and leaving one by one the guards at their positions. That is something I did not see.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When the shooting occurred, you said that was close to the time of the changeover of shifts.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which shooting.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In the "white house," when Crnalic was killed?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, when many people were killed. That was in the evening. I don't know whether it was before midnight or after midnight. Anyway, it was late at night.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I see. Do you know any individuals who were in Krkan's shifts?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Who were they?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know them from before the camp, but I remember Milutin Popovic and Ranko, the electrician, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In which shift were they?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe they were in Krkan's shift. I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you talk to the investigator and did you tell him something different?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may have done so. I don't know. I didn't have an opportunity to read the list and talk to the commander. I know that Ranko, the electrician, and Milutin were in the shift that was the worst one.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Were you able to conclude who was in charge of bringing those people to the camp and releasing the people from the camp?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't able to conclude that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Were you able to establish the chain of command as regards the guards and the inspectors? Who was superior or answerable to whom?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The guards took people for interrogations. I don't know whether they were part of the security staff of Omarska. I don't know. But the guards worked in shifts, and they were the ones who took people for Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. interrogations.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Were there any special groups of guards who were in charge of taking people to interrogations?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know that, because I never saw those people, and I didn't know what kind of function they had in Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You spoke about a machine-gun which was on one of the roofs, and you also said that you had seen the accused in the vicinity.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but it was not them. It was one of the guards who was near the machine-gun nest. The accused were not there at the placement of the machine-gun.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: No. That is not what I said, Witness. Let me rephrase the question. You said that at some point in time, you saw those people on the roof.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What I should like to know, in respect of that, was the following: Was someone always at the machine-gun placement?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: During the day and during the night?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember mostly the individual nicknamed Crni, who used to give us cigarettes and cookies.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: But he would be relieved from time to time?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Probably there were shifts. He must have been relieved from time to time.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In response to a Prosecutor, you said that some were present, and then later on you said that all of the commanders were present. I didn't quite understand you.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand you now.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Would you see them together?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I wanted to clarify, Witness. So you would never see them all together?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Except during the changeover of duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You mentioned an incident involving spilling of some dish-washing powder or detergent.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What was it used for, for washing?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for washing dishes, the dishes that we washed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So you washed the dishes with a washing powder.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but it was a dish-washing powder, not a washing-machine powder.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Witness. Your Honours, I don't have any further questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Fila. Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours, for giving us the floor, but we do not have any questions for Mr. Mesanovic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Stojanovic. Mr. Jovan Simic. MR. J. SIMIC: [Interpretation] No questions for the witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Mr. Keegan, do you have any additional questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, briefly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Mesanovic, yesterday when you were being

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: functioning of your office, the Mobilisation Unit, and he raised the issue of the mobilisation of equipment. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: You testified in detail about how that was done, that notices would be sent out and that the equipment could even include personal vehicles. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: During the time that you were still working in the Mobilisation Unit, that would be up to 24 June 1992, to your knowledge, was there ever an order sent out directing the mobilisation of personal vehicles, that is, personal cars?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: During that same time, that is, up to 24 June, were you aware of the fact that Muslims had had their personal vehicles taken nonetheless?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, including my vehicle as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: During that same time, were you aware of any Serb who had his vehicle confiscated in a similar manner?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Keegan. Judge Fouad Riad has the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Mesanovic. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Perhaps you can be in a position to help me understand more of the conditions in the camp, especially with your experience before in the police. I would like to start by asking you from the beginning. You are married to a Serb. Were people married to a Serb in a better position than other Muslims?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Then I will ask you about your going to Omarska. You said that the worst shift -- when you arrived, they told you the worst shift would come next evening because they have a party where the detainees would kneel against the wall and would be beaten and would be jumped over and so on. Which shift was that?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you that because it was only my second day in Omarska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You did not find out about it later? It was not a weekly celebration?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I really cannot tell you. I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: What about what you called Black Friday? Was it also a weekly celebration?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That happened on a Friday. I don't know what was the reason for that. There was no reason whatsoever. I think that -- we were all very badly beaten up. Usually we would get a kick or a slap here and there, but this time everyone was beaten up. And it was also done on the way back, which hadn't been the case previously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You said that two men, Ranko and Milutin, were in the worst shift. Which shift was that?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was Krkan's shift.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Did you mean that Ranko and Milutin were, themselves, among the worst people, or was it the shift?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The two of them were in my area. They were in charge of the "glass house" and the restaurant. I couldn't tell you about the others because I was not in the hangar or the "white house" or the large sleeping room or the small garage at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, you said that apparently Meakic was kind to you and he sent you to the "glass house" area --

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: -- with four more fighters from Vukovar. Do you think these people were better treated than the others?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: They were. But you said they had no roof on your head. You say the rain would come to you.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: What happened then? You stayed wet inside?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We would take shelter under the overhang but we had to stand up in order to avoid the rain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And also Meakic gave you four names for people you can perhaps ask for help, Krkan, Krle, Ckalja. Did they help you in any way?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't personally ask any one of them for help. Krle, Krkan, and others know about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You did not try and they refused?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You mentioned an incident of Dr. Begic. If I understood rightly, he was under the protection of Krle, but Krkan took him to the "white house." Could you explain that to me, and what happens when one is protected by a shift leader? Does he really benefit or he's like all the others?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I said that Krkan had taken him, but I believe that he was under Krle's protection. However, shifts were 12 hours long, and for the remaining hours there were two other shifts that would be on duty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, my question is this: When somebody is under the protection of a shift leader, is this respected? Is a shift leader respected when he protects someone? You gave the example of Begic but in other cases -- you were under the protection, apparently, of Meakic. So how influential were the shift leaders? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very much so, probably.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Judge Riad. Madam Judge Wald has the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I have just a few questions, Witness. One, you told us that you were beaten during an interrogation by, I believe, an interrogator named Zoric. I think that's what you testified. My question is --

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: My question is: Were there any of the regular camp guards in the room during the interrogation or was it just you and the interrogators?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no guards in my room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Right. Did you hear from other prisoners whether the situation was the same with them? If they were beaten during interrogation, was it, according to what they said, by the regular interrogators or were the regular guards sometimes called in to do the beating, or do you know?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the stories by detainees, guards would enter the rooms. I don't know whether they were the guards belonging to that particular shift. That I don't know. But they were not investigators. So in the presence of investigators, the guards, or I don't know how to call them, servants of the investigators, would beat the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: My next question is in telling us about the incident of the shooting of Crnalic, the English transcript was a little confusing, and maybe you could straighten it out for me. The English transcript said that as Crnalic stood up to go towards the guard it said, "fire was opened," and then it said, "the guard also opened fire." I just want to know who fired first? Was it the guard or was fire from some other place first and then the guard firing came later?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The guards were the ones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: So there was more than one guard that opened fire. Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: My last question is: You told us that you didn't see Mr. Kvocka around the camp after the first part of July, or you may have said the middle of July, but at least -- then you said he was replaced by Mr. Prcac. Can you tell me when -- approximately, when was the first time you saw Mr. Prcac around the camp?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said yesterday that it was the end of the first half of July and that he was replaced by Drago Prcac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: So I'm just verifying this. Was that the first time, around the middle of July, that you saw Mr. Prcac? Yes?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mesanovic, I also have a few questions for you. Let me begin with a very simple question. Were there any civilians who worked in Omarska at the time?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you tell us who they were?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that those were the civilians who were on duty, that is, who had their work obligation there and who work on the maintenance in the came. Pesevic, for example, was driving the yellow truck, and he was driving the bodies away from the "white house" and the "red house." I knew him because he was from Donja Puharska. He was in charge of driving the bodies in a small yellow TAM truck. I think that they would stay in the camp for three days, that their shifts were three days long. Then after that they would go home and come back again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [no translation]

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that there was even a cleaning lady there. She was in charge of cleaning the administration building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [no translation] If a civilian person would be working in the camp, would that person have to wear a military uniform or not? Let me rephrase my question, or rather, repeat my question in case there has been a problem with interpretation. Mr. Mesanovic, in case of civilians working there, if an individual had a work obligation in the camp and if that work obligation consisted of some security work, would that person be required to wear a uniform or not?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We never had people who had a military obligation to provide security for the camp. That was not according to the regulations of the former JNA. I'm referring to the guards who ensured the security of the camp. Second, all similar organisations such as the mine company and others had their own security personnel, and those people also had their work obligation, but they were in charge of providing security to the facility itself, not to the people detained in that facility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me take an example. In case of defence, if individuals have a work obligation in the area of defence, are they required to wear a military uniform or not?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another question. Did you actually see any civilians who were in charge of providing security in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not. They were all wearing uniforms, so I couldn't recognise them. Pesevic was the only one who didn't have any weapons, so that was the reason I concluded that he was a civilian, and also the cleaning lady who was a civilian as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Mesanovic, you have just completed your testimony before the Tribunal. Thank you very much for having come here to testify. But before we let you go, I should also like to know whether you have anything to add, whether there has been anything that hasn't been asked of you, anything that you, yourself, wish to say here in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I mean, there are so many things, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Mesanovic, we could spend years here listening to your story. But we have concluded your testimony, your examination here, your testimony. Thank you once again for coming here and have a safe journey back to your place of residence. Let me ask the usher to show the witness out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Normally we have a half-hour break at this time. It is possible that we come a little later than that. But let me say that the break will be half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated. The next witness has asked, through the intermediary of the Prosecution, that protective measures be provided, that is, facial distortion and a pseudonym. The Chamber notes that this request is not, strictly speaking, based on motives of security or serious risk to the private life of the witness. Above all, the Chamber notes that the witness has made it clear that he would agree to testify even if the requested measures of protection were not granted to him. For the Chamber, the principle of the public character of audiences is not called in question except when a closed session hearing is introduced. Other protective measures envisaged by the Rules should be treated as an exception. In this particular case, the Chamber does not feel that there are justifiable reasons for such measures to be granted. The Chamber, however, wishes to pay tribute to the witness for his honesty regarding the way in which his request was made and the efforts he is inclined to make in order to testify in public. We must all be appreciative of his efforts, and as far as we are concerned, the Chamber, the Prosecutor, the Defence, and the public in general will make sure that if necessary, the witness should not, under any circumstances, be a victim of his own honesty. Therefore, the witness will testify without protective measures. Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. Merely before we bring in the next witness, I believe we need to move for the admission of the exhibits for Mr. Mesanovic, which was not done before he left the courtroom. That would be Prosecution Exhibits 118, 119, and 120, the three photographs, and the Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. And there's also the exhibit D32/1 for the Defence. I give the floor to the Defence to see whether they have any objections. Mr. Krstan Simic, he is also requesting the admission of D32/1. I think you have already done that. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I speak on behalf of all Defence. We have no objection to the admission of the exhibits tendered by the Prosecution, and we also wish to tender the Exhibit D32/1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I understand, but I wish to hear it from Mr. Keegan, that you have no objection to the admission ever this Exhibit D32/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case, the quoted exhibits are admitted with the numbers indicated. Mr. Keegan, I see that it is going to be Mr. Saxon who has taken up his position to work today.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The next witness for the Prosecution will be Mr. Omer mesan. The points of direct examination for this witness will be his personal particulars, the conduct of Miroslav Kvocka in the Omarska camp, the conduct of Milojica Kos in the Omarska camp, the conduct of Mladjo Radic in the Omarska camp, the conduct of Dragoljub Prcac in the Omarska camp, and finally the identification of the accused Kvocka, Kos, Radic, and Prcac, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We are now waiting for the witness to enter the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether I'm pronouncing your name correctly. Omer mesan.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think the interpreters pronounced it better than me. In any event, please read the solemn declaration given to you by the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated. First of all, let me thank you for coming. You know that the Chamber has rendered a decision regarding protective measures that you requested, and we wish to express our appreciation for your courage and honesty in accepting to testify in public session. We are all cognisant of this. You are now going to answer questions put to you by Mr. Saxon, who is standing to your right. Mr. Saxon, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Sir, would you please state your full name?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: My name is Omer mesan.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What was the place and the date of your birth?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: I was born on the 27th of September, 1959, in Kupres.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Where were you residing until 1992?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Until 1992, I was residing in Prijedor municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What is your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: I'm a Bosniak Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Are you married?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do you have children?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Two children.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: How old were your children, Mr. Masan, in 1992?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: My older child was 9, and the younger one was 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Masan, were you detained in the Omarska camp during the summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Yes, I was detained.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: How long were you detained in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: From the 31st of May until the 7th of August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: During the first few weeks of your confinement in Omarska, where in the camp were you detained? What part of the camp?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. The first part of my detention was the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: I was at the pista. We spent the nights or the first night at the pista and the other nights, some 10 or 15 nights, in the kitchen. In the first half, we also spent some time in the cloak room used by the workers to change in, the changing rooms.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Approximately how many weeks did you spend on the pista?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: From time to time. Sometimes we would spend some time inside. After the interrogation, I spent about two weeks -- I can't remember exactly -- at the pista.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Approximately how many prisoners were detained on the pista with you?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Depending on the period and on the situation, 500, 600, more or less than that. But the group was rather large.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Masan, prior to your detention in the Omarska camp, did you know a man named Miroslav Kvocka?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you become familiar with Miroslav Kvocka while you were a prisoner at Omarska?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Yes, I became familiar with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: How did you learn Miroslav Kvocka's identity?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: I learnt Miroslav Kvocka's name from the prisoners who were there with me in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: How often would you see Mr. Kvocka during your detention at Omarska?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Just several times? Would that be several times in a day, several times a week, or several times altogether?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Several times during the day or several times in the first month and a half I was in the camp. At all times of day. In the morning, at noon, towards evening, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What was Mr. Kvocka's position at the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Judging by what I was able to observe, Kvocka had a certain command position in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Where would Mr. Kvocka be on the occasions when you saw him?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: I would see him all over the camp, at least every part of the camp that I was able to see. I would see him in front of the administration building, around the "white house," above the administration building, at the very gates, entrance gates. At several places. I would see him walking. I would see him in a car.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What would Mr. Kvocka be doing on these occasions?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: That depended also on the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Did you ever see Mr. Kvocka supervising guards?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Yes, I did see him doing that several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you give an example of how you saw Mr. Kvocka supervising the guards?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: For example, on one or two occasions at least, I saw Kvocka when the evening shift arrived, which would be about half past six in the evening, 18.30. When he would take over the shift, he would line up the guards in two rows and he would stand between them, he would pass between them, explaining something to them which I was not able to hear, and he would walk between them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this point if I would ask the usher to place one of these photographs on the ELMO next to the witness and distribute the remaining copies to the Defence and to the Chamber. One copy could be marked as Prosecution Exhibit 3/121, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Saxon, excuse me for interrupting you, but I should like to take advantage of this pause. To "supervise" is a legal concept. Perhaps it would be better not to use it. This is a minor remark on my part, and I apologise for the interruption.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Which term would you prefer Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that I not use?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The term "supervise." Perhaps you could ask the witness what was the relationship, what was the behaviour, the conduct. "Supervise," I think, is already a legal judgement, a legal conclusion. If you ask what kind of relationship they had, this is more precise. I'm not making an issue out of it, but I think that would be better.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Masan, could you take a look at the photograph that's on the machine next to you.

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do you recognise that?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What does that photograph show?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: In the front of the photograph we see the "white house" or the shed known as the "white house." To the left, that I am pointing to, is the restaurant, and behind it is the administration building, on the top floor. The ground floor was used as changing rooms. In the left-hand corner on the ground floor was a garage. And the building to the right is the so-called hangar. The part between these two buildings is an asphalt area that we called the pista.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Masan, could you take a pen that's in front of you and mark with the letters "OM" the approximate spot on the pista where you would have been when you saw Mr. Kvocka speaking with arriving guards.

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: I stated that I saw him at least twice. Once when I saw Kvocka, I was in front of the room used by the workers to change in, and on both sides of the entrance there are facilities for washing shoes, taps, water taps, and we would gather around them, and Kvocka would take over the guards here. Here. I was here. You can't see the front of the building on this photograph. The second time I was at the pista, near these three concrete objects that used to be used for flowers and plants, and once I was here in this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And what did you observe that Mr. Kvocka was doing on those two occasions when the guards were arriving at the camp?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: When the guards arrived at the camp, they would form two rows.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: The guards would line up and face one another, and between those two lines of guards Miroslav Kvocka would pass and say something to them. I can't say exactly how long this took, five or ten minutes, and then together with them he would move on to their positions where they were to take up duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Masan, could you draw with another pen on that photograph where the two rows of guards would form?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Roughly parallel with this building. In this area here, where I wrote the initials "MK."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And do those initials "MK" stand for Miroslav Kvocka?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If that could be noted for the record, please. And if the initials "OM", also in that photograph, could also be noted for the record as standing for Omer mesan. And if it could be noted that the two orange lines signify rows of guards.

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: In one case, I was standing in front of this building, and I could see that very clearly, because it was straight ahead, straight in front of us. I was roughly here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Masan, on these occasions, would the shift commanders be present as well?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Mostly all those who came by bus were present I didn't notice that any one of the guards would move away earlier or stay behind after the group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, could the question be "Who was present?" Please. Because no mention has been made so far of shift commanders, because the question implies that the shift commanders were there. So, according to the system I'm familiar with, the question, the appropriate question, would be "Who was present?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Saxon. Your response?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I simply asked whether the witness observed whether any shift commanders were present, but I'm willing to rephrase my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, rephrase the question, because otherwise, one could say you were leading the witness. Ask who was present, and then afterwards you may ask what the position of those present was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you recognise anyone else present when the guards were arriving on those occasions?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: You want me to answer the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Yes. I apologise. I recognised all the people who came there. Milojica Kos would come from time to time, a certain individual called Ckalja, then Mladjo Radic, Krkan. I told you that it took place on at least on two occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you. And we will discuss those individuals later on. Were you ever present when guards spoke to Miroslav Kvocka?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Yes, I was present on one occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And what happened on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Miroslav Kvocka was coming out of the administration building. It was in the afternoon, and standing away from me, about between five or ten metres, a guard called him up from this area here, near the hangar. His assignment was here, on this corner. He used to stand guard here very often, and he addressed him as "Boss." And I believe he was referring to him, because Kvocka was standing there and the guard approached him. They talked for a while, and after that they went their own ways, their own separate ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Let's go a little bit slower.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And if I could ask the usher to remove that photograph, please. And if this photograph could be placed on the ELMO, and if a copy could be marked as Prosecution Exhibit 3/122.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Masan, when you say "He addressed him as boss," who was he? Who spoke that day?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I was referring to one the guards - I believe I have already said that - who was standing here, level with this corner. The guards would always be here, and several trucks that were used for the transport of mine ore were there. And the guard was standing right there next to the corner.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And what did the guard -- and where did you see Mr. Kvocka on that day?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Kvocka came out of the administration building, this part here, and was walking in this direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And when Mr. Kvocka came out of the administration building, what did the guard say?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: He called him up - it was very unofficial - and he said, "Hey, boss," something to that effect, and they stopped and talked for a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: When the guard uttered the words "Hey, boss," how, if at all, did Mr. Kvocka react?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: He stopped. He turned around and stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Masan, could you mark with a pen on that photograph approximately where you were on that occasion? Mark the letters "OM", please.

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And can you also mark with the letters "MK" where Mr. Kvocka stopped on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: After Mr. Kvocka stopped, what happened then?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: The guard who had called him went near him, near Kvocka.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What happened then?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: For a while, they talked, and after that they parted. The guard went back to his position and Kvocka went away.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you. If that photograph could be removed now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Masan, could you observe what happened when the interrogators arrived in the camp in the morning?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Yes, I could, on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Who, if anyone, ever welcomed the interrogators to the camp?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Sometimes they would be welcomed in a ceremonious way by Zeljko Meakic, for example, or by Miroslav Kvocka.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And can you describe how Miroslav Kvocka would welcome the interrogators?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Sometimes he would stand in front of the entrance to the administration building and wait for them to pass by, and he would greet them sometimes individually, shake hands with them, and then he would enter the building together with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And apart from Miroslav Kvocka or Zeljko Meakic, did you observe anyone else welcome the interrogators in such a manner?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: No. I cannot say that I observed anyone else doing that in that manner, but there were guards or people who considered themselves as commanders, who would happen to be in front of the administration building at that time, and from time to time they would greet the investigators but not in an official way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Masan, prior to your detention in Omarska, did you know a man named Milojica Kos?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: While you were detained at Omarska, did you become familiar with Milojica Kos?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did Mr. Kos have a nickname?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Yes. They call him Krle.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: How often would you see Mr. Kos in the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Very often. I mean, several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Again, just so that the record is clear, is that several times in a day, in a week, or several times during your confinement in the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Every day. I mean, during the day when Kos was on duty, when his shift was on duty in the camp, I would see him several times. And I used to see him until the Omarska camp -- I mean, until I left the Omarska camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Where would you see Mr. Kos?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: In every part of the camp, what I was able to observe.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do you know what Mr. Kos' position in the Omarska camp was?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Mr. Kos was a shift commander, a commander of one of the shifts.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What led you to conclude that Mr. Kos was a shift commander?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: By the way he behaved. I had the impression that he was a superior in respect to the guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What gave you that impression?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Kos would give assignments to the guards when they came to the camp. Then the kind of freedom of movement enjoyed by Kos in the camp. Then there was also an incident which led me to conclude that he was the one who issued orders to that shift.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go a little bit more slowly if we can. You mentioned the freedom of movement enjoyed by Mr. Kos in the camp. How did the freedom of movement enjoyed by Mr. Kos differ from the freedom of movement enjoyed by ordinary guards?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: I noticed that ordinary guards had their assigned positions, and they would move around that particular area. I also noticed that they had some specific tasks. Whereas one could see Kos in various parts of the camp. He didn't have a specific spot to which he was assigned.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Masan, did you know a prisoner at Omarska named Mehmedalija Nasic?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Yes, I knew him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you know Mr. Nasic before the war?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: How did you know Mr. Nasic?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: He used to live in my neighbourhood, and he would pass by my house every day. I knew his family as well. I knew his brother.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What was Mr. Nasic's ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: He was a Bosniak Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What happened to Mr. Mehmedalija Nasic at Omarska?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Mehmedalija Nasic, on one particular night when we were brought to the restaurant to spend the night, was killed on one of the tables inside the restaurant, with a shot coming from the outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: When you say Mr. Nasic was killed with a shot coming from the outside, how exactly did that shot enter the restaurant?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: A guard by the name of Pavlic had opened fire from outside the restaurant, and he killed Nasic and injured two or three other people. At least two.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did Mr. Pavlic fire through a window?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Yes, through the glass.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And what happened to the glass window as a result?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Of course the glass was broken. There was a hole in the window after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do you know what guard shift Mr. Pavlic was on?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: In Milojica Kos' shift, Milojica Kos, called Krle.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Masan, how far from Mehmedalija Nasic were you when he was shot?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: I was in that room, two or three metres away from it. I don't know exactly how far, but it was really very near to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Sometime after the death of Mehmedalija Nasic, what, if anything, did Mr. Kos say to the detainees in the restaurant?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: After awhile, after this unfortunate incident, at that time, it was the evening shift, from 7.00 p.m. until 7.00 a.m. Sometime after that, Kos came to the door of the restaurant, and he stood inside of the restaurant, and he asked that the detainees who were there collect 27 billion dinars. And he said -- I cannot quote him, but he said something to the effect, "You will soon be going home, leaving the camp, and Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. somebody will have to pay for this glass. The price is 27 billion dinars. You better collect the money. I'm not going to pay for it." Those were his exact words.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Just so the record is clear, you said that Mr. Kos asked that the detainees collect 27 billion dinars. Did Mr. Kos' comment come in the form of a request or in some or form?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Yes. Kos requested that money, that is 27 million dinars to be collected. And such requests, according to what we had experienced before, were very dangerous and perilous. Many people perished after such requests.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did the prisoner -- let me go more slowly. Mr. Masan, were you present in the restaurant that evening?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I was in the restaurant.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did the prisoners collect the 27 billion dinars?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: I don't know whether they collected exactly 27 billion dinars, but a sum of money was very quickly collected.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Who did the prisoners give this money to?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: One of the guards who was in the corridor at the entrance to the administration building was called up, because at that time there were two guards in the corridor, and the money was handed over to one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: After the money was given to this guard, what happened next?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Shortly after that, maybe a half hour later, a guard by the name of Jokic came, and he returned the money.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you know Mr. Jokic before the war?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: No, no. I came to know him in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What did Mr. Jokic look like?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: He was rather thin, and he was wearing a police uniform, the kind that was worn by the reserve contingent of the police. He was not taller than 180 centimetres, I think. He had a longish face.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do you know Mr. Jokic's profession?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: I heard from people who knew him that he was a butcher.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What, if anything, did Mr. Jokic have in his hand when Mr. Jokic entered the room?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: I don't remember. I just remember him bringing in the money. I don't recall any objects that he may have had in his hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What, if anything, did Mr. Jokic say when he brought the money back into the restaurant?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Yes, he did. He said, "Here is the money. I cannot watch this any longer. I cannot stand this," and he gave the money to one of the prisoners standing next to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: How did the prisoners in the room react when Mr. Jokic returned the money?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: There was a certain relief, almost a kind of euphoria. The prisoners started applauding.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Had any stolen goods been returned to prisoners previously?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know of any such instances that anything would be returned to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Following this incident, did you ever see stolen property returned to prisoners again?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: No, never. Nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Masan, do you know whose shift Mr. Jokic was assigned to at the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me. Mr. Krstan Simic, what is your objection? MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I should like to object to the question. Mr. Saxon is asking the witness whether the property was returned without asking whether the property had ever been stolen. We believe that this is an example of a leading question. He's talking about the return of property, and we still do not know whether such property had been taken away from the detainees in the first place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, certainly there has been ample evidence and testimony provided in this trial that property was removed from prisoners, certainly at the very least, under duress, and the witness is -- MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we're talking about facts here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And the Prosecution would argue that property taken under duress is the equivalent of stolen property, Your Honour. I see nothing wrong with my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Saxon, that is certainly true, but it is also true that you haven't yet asked the witness the first question. Would you please rephrase your question; otherwise, you will be leading the witness indeed. I know we are always faced with this problem involving a speedy trial. We try to work as quickly as possible. However, there are questions which are not essential and which can be somehow skipped, and we can ask the witness to respond with either "yes" or "no"; however, when we are dealing with essential questions concerning this particular case, the situation is different. We had an example here when the word "supervise" was mentioned and when the phrase "shift leader" was used. That is very important, and it is very difficult to avoid leading the witness in such cases. But this is a different situation. Of course, leading questions will never be allowed; however, we also risk wasting a lot of time. So there has to be a balance here, and we have to maintain certain criteria. I'm going to ask Mr. Saxon to rephrase his question. It is true that we have heard a number of witnesses say the same thing, but we have this witness here for the first time. So I have to ask you, Mr. Saxon, to rephrase your question, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will do that very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Masan, following this incident, did you ever see property taken from prisoners?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Yes, before that and after that. Various kinds of objects were seized under threats of beatings: jewellery, rings, chains, jackets, footwear. Various property, including cigarettes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Following this, did you ever see property returned to prisoners?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: No, never. I never saw any property being returned to anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do you know whose shift Mr. Jokic was assigned to at the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: He was on the same shift as Milojica Kos, called Krle.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What, if anything, happened the following morning?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: The following morning, between, I don't know, 6.00 and 7.00, as we were getting out of the restaurant I noticed Jokic and Krle, that is, Milojica Kos, called Krle, standing in front of the administration building on an elevated area, discussing the incident that had taken place the previous night.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Masan, I'm going to interrupt you there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If I could again ask the usher, please, to place this photograph on the ELMO and mark one of as them Prosecution's Exhibit 3/123, and the remaining photographs can be distributed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Masan, could you please take a look at the photograph on the machine next to you. Do you recognise that building?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What building is that?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: This is the administration building and the restaurant.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Just so the record --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry to interrupt you, Mr. Saxon, but this is a kind of situation where you could have asked the witness "Is this the administration building and the restaurant?" Not that it is very important, I just wanted to give an example. You may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Just so the record is clear, how did you leave the restaurant that morning?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: We left the restaurant stepping over this first window, the first window of the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And then where were you going?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: We would go to this area in front of the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If the record can please reflect that the witness is noting the area of the pista.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You mentioned that you saw Mr. Kos and Mr. Jokic that morning when you left the restaurant. Can you take a pen and mark the letters "KOS" where you saw Mr. Kos, please?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you hear the conversation going on between the two men?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What did you hear?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Kos said, I'm not quoting him but words to this effect, "You want to help them, and they would like to slit your throat, the fuckers." Now I'm quoting: "You'll no longer be a part of my shift." That was the context of Kos' words.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: When Mr. Kos made this comment to Mr. Jokic, approximately how far were you from Mr. Kos?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: That was just when I was walking in this direction, crossing from the window and going to the pista. About four or five metres away. Five metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Could you please place the letters "OM" in the approximate area where you were that morning when you heard this remark?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Let me draw a line and my initials.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What, if anything, did Mr. Kos say to the prisoners on the pista at that time?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: The mistreatment started then.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, perhaps you didn't understand the question. I'll rephrase it. What, if anything, did Mr. Kos say to the prisoners at that time?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: He cursed them, their Turkish mothers, and all kinds of other vulgar expressions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: After this discussion between Mr. Kos and Mr. Jokic, approximately how much time remained on Kos' shift, guard shift, that morning?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: This was towards the end, the very end. Maybe there was an hour left or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: During that hour, the following hour, how were the prisoners treated at that time?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: They forced people to face the wall, to lie down. They cursed them and that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: During that hour, what sounds, if any, could you hear coming from other parts of the camp?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Masan, did you ever see Mr. Kos when you went to the restaurant for your daily meal?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: I did see him several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could ask the usher to help me again. If the photograph currently on the ELMO could be removed, and if a copy of this photograph could be placed on the ELMO and a copy marked as Prosecution Exhibit 3/124. The witness will also be annotating this exhibit. And other copies may be distributed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Masan, if you could take a look at the photograph that's been placed on the ELMO. Which entrance or entrances would you use to enter the building, the restaurant building, for your daily meal?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Every day we used the entrance in between these two pillars. That is the entrance. We would pass in between these two pillars.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: When, if ever, would you enter that building through the side entrance?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: In the evenings, when we went to sleep inside, we would enter across the window, in some cases. If we were staying in this area, the ground floor and the changing rooms, then we would enter them through this door that is visible on the side.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: When you entered the building through the side entrance, did you ever see Mr. Kos?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Yes, several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And can you recall what Mr. Kos said to the prisoners on any of those occasions?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: I remember cost mostly by the diligence with which he mistreated people. He had a stick that he carried with him, or a cable. On one occasion when we were sitting here, in front of this door, a small group of us, there was a prisoner. I think, by the way Kos addressed him, he was a school friend of his made Atko. And one occasion he said, "Fuck Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. your balija mothers. Why aren't you like my friend Atko, then this wouldn't happen to you." I don't know what kind of man Atko was nor what he meant by this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Just so the record is clear, who is "he"?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Kos said to one of the prisoners who, if I remember well, was called Atko.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you mark with your pen the approximate place where Mr. Kos was by that entrance, please, with the letters "KOS", K-O-S.

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: When, if ever, was Mr. Kos present when you entered or exited the restaurant building through the front entrance that's underneath -- that's close to the circular window?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: He was mostly there in the period from 9.00 until 3.00 in the afternoon. That was when the meal was served. And on several occasions I would see him here, in this area, moving around.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What Mr. Kos be doing at the time during that mealtime?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: I noticed, on a number of occasions, that he would hit somebody or one of the prisoners several times during the period I spent in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What, if anything, would Mr. Kos use to hit the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: He had a kind of stick which could be attached to the arm. Something like a cable, an object like that. I remember well. He wore gloves without fingers, and he used this stick mostly to hit with.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Masan, could you take that pen again and mark with the letters "KOS" the approximate areas where you would see Mr. Kos on those occasions.

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And how far from Mr. Kos would you be on those occasions?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: About 15 metres away, because the distance between the two buildings is about 20, 25 metres. So these things were mostly happening here in front because that's where people were lining up waiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Were you still detained on the pista at this time?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Yes, mostly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you. If that photograph could be removed now. Can we have that photograph placed again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Masan, just so the record is clear, could you put the number 1 by the letters "KOS" that are by the side entrance?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And the number 2 by the letters "KOS" by the other entrance. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If that photograph could be removed now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Masan, prior your detention in the Omarska camp, did you know a man by the name of Mladjo Radic?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you become familiar with a man named Mladjo Radic during the time you were detained in the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: I did. I got to know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What was Mr. Radic's nickname in the Omarska came?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: They called him Krkan.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If you know, what was Mr. Radic's position in the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: I was able to observe that Radic had a superior position in relation to the guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And what led you to conclude that Mr. Radic had a superior position?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: When the shift would arrive to work, so to speak, Radic would go in front of them or to the side of them. They would walk in twos. And when they arrived in front of the administration building, Radic would distribute the guards. And in the course of my stay in the camp, I was able to observe that Radic had control, that he had a certain freedom of movement in the camp. I would frequently see him entering or coming out of the administration building or in the part of the administration building, that is, the window at the top of the staircase, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: When you say that Radic would distribute the guards, what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: He would show the guards where they should go. It was very rare for the guards to change their positions. But one could clearly notice that he was the one telling them where they should go, where they should keep watch.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you ever observe Mlado Radic taking prisoners from one part of the Omarska camp to another.

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What happened on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: On one occasion, one of the incidents I saw was in the early evening. But let me add that my impression was that the largest number of call-outs of prisoners occurred when Radic's shift was on duty. Once I saw a group of five or, rather, seven prisoners being taken by Mladjo Radic from the building that was used as changing rooms, where we were detained, in the direction of the "white house." He led them across the pista. He carried a list in his hand, and he led this group of seven. A man, whose name I think was Halimid, appeared the next day or, rather, during the night I think he was captured. And one of the men who was taken away was a man called Baltic, nicknamed Uca, who lived in a neighbourhood called Pecani in Prijedor. He was a locksmith, I think, by trade. And those men never returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If I could ask the usher to place a photograph on the ELMO again, please, and if a copy of this photograph could be marked as Prosecution 3/125.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Masan, if you could take a look at the photograph on the machine next to you, please. Where were you when you observed Mr. Radic on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: I was in this part of the pista here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Could you mark that spot with the letters "OM", please. And could you show on that photograph the room from which Mr. Radic began escorting prisoners at that time?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: From this room here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Could you mark that spot with a "R1", please.

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And what did you see Mr. Radic do when you left the area of that room?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
