utterances.text: I saw Radic going along with those prisoners, escorting them in the direction of the "white house." I didn't see Radic call them out, I just saw him accompanying them along this route.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Could you mark with a "R2" the spot where you last saw Mr. Radic and this group of prisoners, please.

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: It was roughly opposite the entrance to the administration building.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you. If that photograph could be removed now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Masan, where else would you see Mr. Radic in the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: All over the camp, that I was able to observe.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you ever see Mr. Radic present when prisoners were mistreated?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What happened on that occasion? Where were you?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: I was at the pista.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What happened on that day?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: On that day, when the meal was being distributed, all the groups in the camp were mistreated, beaten. A group of guards lined up at the entrance and in the corridor inside, and prisoners were beaten going in for lunch and going out. I was among them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And when, if ever, on that day did you see Mr. Radic?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: I saw him roughly around midday. I can't tell you exactly what time it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And where was Mr. Radic when you saw him?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: When I saw him -- but this went on for some time. It was like a show. He was standing in the glass area, on the staircase inside the administration building. He was accompanied at least by one person wearing a military camouflage uniform. I spent some time there then. Some prisoners, out of fear, didn't want to go and eat. Many had very serious injuries on their head, face, shoulders. People were beaten up with cables, chains, truncheons, guns. It was terrible.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Just so that the record is clear, Mr. Masan, when you say this went on for some time, what went on for some time?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: The beatings. Very severe beatings went on throughout the period during which the lunch was distributed. All groups were beaten on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If I could again ask the usher to place this photograph on the ELMO, and if a copy could be marked as Prosecution Exhibit 3/126. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Masan, if you could please take a look at the photograph that's been placed next to you. When you saw Mr. Radic on that day, where was Mr. Radic?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Radic was here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you mark that spot with the letters "MR", please?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And approximately where were you that day when these beatings were going on?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Throughout that day, I was on the pista here. You can't see the building, but it's just here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Could you mark with the letters "OM" the approximate spot where you were at the time, please?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Masan, on that day, to your knowledge, did Mr. Radic do anything to stop those beatings?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: I didn't notice anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you hear Mr. Radic say anything to the guards who were committing those beatings?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: I didn't notice him saying anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you. If that photograph could be removed now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Masan, prior to your detention in the Omarska camp, did you know a man named Dragoljub Prcac?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you become familiar with Mr. Prcac while you were confined in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: How did you learn who Mr. Prcac was?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: I learnt it from the prisoners who were with me in the Omarska camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: When you saw Mr. Prcac in the Omarska camp, what, if anything, would he be doing?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: I saw him on several occasions, but what I seem to remember very well is that Prcac would always be handling some kind of lists, paperwork, carrying around these documents and lists.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: How would you describe Mr. Prcac's demeanour at the times when you saw him in the camp?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: I don't know how to put it. He was sort of formal. He didn't pay much attention to his surroundings.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you recall the events of the last day that you spent in the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What happened in Omarska that day?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: On that day, prisoners were called out. One group was sent to the pista, another group to the garage, and a third in front of the building where we were detained.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Masan, when you refer to groups of prisoners, how big were these groups, approximately?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: That depended on the group. At the end, the group of prisoners on the pista numbered about 600 to 700 men. The group that I was a part of that were called out were 1.250 or something like that. And the group that remained in the camp numbered about 160 to 170 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And that morning, were there any prisoners who were not put into a particular group?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Yes. I noticed, during the call-out, that some prisoners had been taken to the pista or, rather, were called out even though we knew they had been killed. Then there was a group of some 50 men who were not on any of the lists. They were some sort of a surplus.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If I could ask Mr. Usher again, please, if he could place this photograph on the ELMO, and if it could be marked as Prosecution 3/127.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Saxon, I don't know whether it would be convenient for you to have a break now. Maybe you have something to finish off before the break, or whether a pause would suit you now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may have just a few moments now and then it will be a most convenient time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Would you please take a look at that photograph, Mr. Masan, and mark with the lowers "OM" where you were that morning, where you were taken out.

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: I was taken out early in the afternoon. This was happening early in the afternoon. The call-out started in the morning, and it went on into the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You mentioned a group of 50 prisoners who were not included in any of these lists. What happened when the guards realised that there were 50 prisoners who were not included in any list?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: One of the guards said, rather angrily, "Fuck it. Fifty men are not listed anywhere." And he addressed Prcac personally. I don't remember who the guard was, but I know that he addressed him to Prcac.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you see Mr. Prcac at this time?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Yes, I did see him. He participated. Stanko Krivaja had one list, and Drago Prcac had another list.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: But at this moment, when the guard spoke to Mr. Prcac, could you see Mr. Prcac?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I could see him. He was very close to me, about five or six metres away from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Could you mark on that photograph the letters "DP" approximately where Mr. Prcac was.

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What, if anything, did Mr. Prcac say at that time?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: I don't remember his immediate reaction, but I know that Drago Prcac brought those 50 men and placed them in the garage and said, "This is easy to deal with. I have resolved the problem." That is what he said. And he brought those men to the garage in the back part of the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If the record could reflect that the witness has pointed to a corner of the administration building on the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Masan, how did the guards treat Mr. Prcac, to use your expression, as he resolved this problem?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: There was no reaction, positive or negative. I think they were indifferent, that Drago Prcac acted independently. There was no reaction.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And later that day, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: In the afternoon, we were boarded onto buses and taken to Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And just so that the record is clear, when you say that on this occasion Drago Prcac brought these 50 men and placed them in the garage, where did Drago Prcac bring these 50 men from?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: This group of men had been brought from this area, that is, the area in between. They were not staying on the pista. I think they were collected from these rooms, but they came from this direction between the two buildings. I saw them being brought from over there, from between those two buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: May the record please reflect that the witness is referring to the hangar and the administration building. Your Honour, if this would be a convenient time to stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I'll ask the usher to accompany the witness out, please. And we're going to have a half-hour break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may be seated. Yes, Mr. Saxon, I think that we are ready to continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Masan, after you left the Omarska camp, where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: We were taken to the Manjaca camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And from Manjaca, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: From Manjaca, after about 15 or 16 days, I was transferred to the Trnopolje camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: How long were you detained in Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: For approximately ten days. I don't know exactly for how long.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And following your release from Trnopolje, eventually did you leave Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Masan, can you describe how Miroslav Kvocka looked when you saw him in 1992?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: The first time in the camp in 1992 -- that was when I saw him for the first time -- he was wearing a blue police camouflage uniform. He had heavy-duty police boots, a beret on his head, a police beret. He was armed with a pistol. I'm not familiar with weapons, but it had an ammunition clip like this. It was a fairly large type of pistol, and he had a collapsible handle. He was wearing a belt with handcuffs suspended from that belt. A police attire.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: About how tall would you say Mr. Kvocka was?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Approximately 180 centimetres. I think that was his height, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Now would you describe his build.

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: He was rather slim, and you could see his curly hair coming out underneath his beret. He was of an athletic build.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Masan, have you seen Miroslav Kvocka since you left the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you describe that occasion or occasions, please?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: It happened at the beginning of October, on the 10th of October, 1992. I saw Miroslav Kvocka in the company of Zeljko Meakic. They were coming from the direction of the police station in Prijedor, and they were passing by the tax service building. I don't know what is the current use of that building, but I saw them there. Both of them were wearing a police uniform at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And on any other occasion since leaving the Omarska camp have you seen Mr. Kvocka?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Not live.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, let's talk about in the media. Have you seen Mr. Kvocka in the media?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Yes, I have seen him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you describe in what context that occurred, please?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Immediately after the arrest of Kvocka, I saw him give a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And how did you see Mr. Kvocka give a statement?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: I cannot quote his words, but he gave a statement to the TV saying that he was not guilty of the charges brought against him, that his was a mixed marriage, and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And since that time, have you seen Mr. Kvocka on television on other occasions?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: No, not that I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Although eight years have passed since your confinement in the Omarska camp, do you think that you could identify the person that you knew as Miroslav Kvocka today?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Masan, could you please look around the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me. Mr. Simic, what is the objection? MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the witness has clearly said that he saw Mr. Kvocka on TV. The question was whether, after eight years, the witness would be able to recognise him. It is obvious that the witness has had an opportunity to see Mr. Kvocka. I just wanted it to be stated clearly that he actually saw him on TV, which was two and a half years ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but have you heard the answer of the witness, Mr. Simic? MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] No. No, I haven't heard the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps, Mr. Saxon, you could repeat the last question, because Mr. Simic hasn't heard the answer provided by the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: My question was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The answer is on the transcript, Mr. Simic. Mr. Saxon, but go ahead. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there must have been a misunderstanding. I didn't hear the answer because I intervened before, and my objection was -- concerned actually the time when he last saw him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Maybe you're too precise, Mr. Simic. But let us hear the question once again, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Masan, although eight years have passed since your confinement in the Omarska camp, do you think that you could identify the person that you knew as Miroslav Kvocka today?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please continue, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Masan, could you please look around the courtroom to determine if you can identify the person whom you referred to in your testimony as Miroslav Kvocka?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: I can. He is sitting between Mladjo Radic and Kos.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you describe what the gentleman is wearing?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: He's wearing a tie; there's a tie around his neck. He's wearing a black blazer and a blue shirt.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And where is that gentleman in reference to the security guard on our left-hand side?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: He's the third one sitting in the row, the first one being Mladjo Radic, and next to him is Miroslav Kvocka. If we take the guard as the first person in the row, Mladjo Radic is the second one and Miroslav Kvocka the third one. But looking from the other side is the same, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Is there any doubt in your mind that the person you identified is the person you knew in the Omarska camp as Miroslav Kvocka?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: I'm absolutely sure that it is one and the same person.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If the record could please reflect that the witness has identified the accused Kvocka.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Masan, can you describe how Milojica Kos looked when you saw him in 1992?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Milojica Kos, on several occasions, because I cannot say that he wore the same kind of uniform throughout my time in the camp, but for a while he wore a pair of blue jeans, a military camouflage jacket without sleeves, black gloves without fingers. That would be the kind of clothing he wore.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: About how tall was he?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: One metre seventy, one metre eighty, thereabouts. He was somewhat shorter than Kvocka.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: How would you describe Mr. Kos' build?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: He was also slim in respect to his height, between 70 and 80 kilos. He had dark hair, straight black hair.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Masan, have you seen Milojica Kos since you left the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: No. No, I haven't seen him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Have you seen Mr. Kos at any time in the media since you left the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: No, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Although eight years have passed since your confinement in the Omarska camp, do you think that you could identify the person you knew as Milojica Kos today?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Yes, I could.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Masan, could you please look around the courtroom to determine if you can identify the person who you refer to in your testimony as Milojica Kos.

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Yes. He's sitting to Kvocka's left. Milojica Kos is sitting to the left-hand side of Miroslav Kvocka.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you describe what that gentleman is wearing today? Stand up if you need to.

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: He's wearing a blue shirt, a blue blazer, I think it is, and a tie, which is also blue but in a different hue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Is there any doubt in your mind that the person that you've just identified is the person you knew in the Omarska camp as Milojica Kos?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: No. No doubt whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: May the record please reflect that the witness has identified the accused Kos.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Masan, can you describe how Mladjo Radic looked when you saw him in 1992 in the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: He wore a police uniform, an uni-coloured police uniform. He had a police beret on his head. He was rather dark, fat, with a big belly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: How tall was he?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Not taller than 1 metre 80 or thereabouts, but I think that he weighed over a hundred kilos.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: When you say he wore a police uniform, an uni-coloured police uniform, do you remember the colour?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: It was blue, except that the trousers were of a darker shade of blue, and the shirt was a lighter shade of blue with short sleeves. It was a summer type of police uniform. And he was armed with a kind of automatic weapon, a short piece of automatic weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Masan, have you seen Mladjo Radic since you left the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: No, I haven't seen him since I left the Omarska camp. However, at the beginning of 1993 or maybe 1994, we could see some programme about the Omarska camp, and I saw the same footage, the same clip when Mladjo Radic was filmed outside the entrance to the administration building, actually, near the circular stairway, but I didn't see him live. And for the past four or five years I haven't seen him on TV either.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Masan, did you also see a photograph of Mr. Radic recently while you were in the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Yes, I did. The photograph that I spoke about.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could simply ask the usher to place this photograph on the ELMO. I've provided a copy to Mr. Radic's counsel previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If you could take a look at this photograph. Is that the photograph that you briefly saw recently?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Yes. That is exactly the photograph that was broadcast on TV, and that's the one that I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If that photograph could be removed now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Masan --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me. What is going to be the number of the document, Mr. Saxon?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no intention of marking that photograph. I simply wanted to bring it to the Court's attention and the accused's attention, which I have done; that's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you. I think we already have that photograph with a number on it. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That photograph has already been admitted into evidence, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Masan, although eight years have passed since your confinement in the Omarska camp, do you think that you could identify the person that you knew as Mladjo Radic today?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Yes, I think I could.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Please look around the courtroom, then, to determine if you can identify the person who you referred to in your testimony as Mladjo Radic.

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: It's the man sitting to Kvocka's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you describe what that man is wearing?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: He's wearing a grey blazer, his shirt is red, and he has a checkered tie.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Is there any doubt in your mind that the person who you identified is the person that you knew in the Omarska camp as Mladjo Radic?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: No doubt.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: May the record please reflect that the witness has identified the accused Mr. Radic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Masan, can you describe how Dragoljub Prcac looked when you saw him in 1992?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Dragoljub Prcac also wore a police uniform consisting of blue trousers, dark blue trousers, and a light blue shirt.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: About how tall was he?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: One metre seventy, one metre eighty; quite big.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: How would you describe his weight or his build?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Between 80 and 90 kilos, I'd say.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you notice anything about Mr. Prcac's hair?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: I don't understand what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What kind of hair did he have, if he had hair?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Oh, I see. Dark hair.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What kind of complexion did Mr. Prcac have?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: It was rather dark, rather dark complexion. Very characteristic features, sharp face features.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Have you seen Dragoljub Prcac since you left the Omarska camp in 1992?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: No, I have not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Although eight years have passed since your confinement in the Omarska camp, do you think that you could identify the person who you knew as Dragoljub Prcac today?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: I think I could.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Masan, could you please look around the courtroom to determine if you can identify the person who you referred to in your testimony as Dragoljub Prcac?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: No. He's not here. I haven't noticed him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this point I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Saxon. Mr. Simic, Krstan Simic, what is going to be the order of the cross-examination? MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the order will be somewhat different. Mr. Kos' counsel will be the first to cross-examine the witness, I shall follow, and then afterwards we will follow the order of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. Mr. O'Sullivan, it's your turn. Your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: May it please the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Sir, you testified that you knew Mehmedalija Nasic before the war. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: You were from the same neighbourhood, and you were friends with him and his family; is that right?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: We were not friends, but I knew his family. Mr. Nasic would pass daily in front of the house where I lived, and so did his brother, Vahid Nasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Sir, you testified about a shooting through a large glass window. The shot shattered the window, it killed Nasic and wounded two or three others. Would you agree that that was a most dramatic event?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: It is certainly something that a person who saw it would never forget.

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Of course not.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I'd like to move to a different area and ask you some questions. When did you first meet with representatives of the Prosecution of the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly. Quite a long time ago. Maybe two years ago. I don't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Does May 1998 sound about right?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Could be.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: How was that meeting arranged?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: I requested it. I wanted to make a statement before the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: How long in advance did you know that this meeting would take place?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Weeks? Months?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: I was contacted in writing by the Tribunal telling me who to address. Then I contacted the local police. They gave me the address. I wrote to the Tribunal, and after about maybe a month, the Tribunal gave me instructions who to talk to, and I acted accordingly; I addressed myself to that person. And I think this whole procedure lasted about a month, a month and a half.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Before you gave the interview in 1998, had you discussed what you would say with anyone?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Now, when you met with the Prosecutor, how many people were present?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: An interpreter and two persons: one who conducted the interview and another who was present.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And this meeting was conducted over more than one day; is that right?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: No, but it lasted a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Basically a full working day with regular breaks; does that sound about right?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: I can't tell you exactly how long it lasted but from the morning until the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Now, during this interview, was someone writing things down or was there someone working at a computer taking down what was said?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Yes. The person interviewing me took notes of my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: During this interview, you were asked questions to which you responded. Was that the basic format?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: There were questions, but there were also my own statements that were not prompted by questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes. So you offered information without specifically being prompted by a question?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Yes. I provided information, because the very fact that I applied was not prompted by anything else but my own free will. If I have made myself clear, there were questions and there were also my own statements freely given.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: So during the interview, you spoke freely?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Absolutely freely, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And no one stopped you from speaking?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: No. No one stopped me, nor did they lead me in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And you did not withhold or hide any information from them, did you?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Let me tell you, the Omarska camp is something that you can refer to daily with new memories because it is difficult to cover everything. Things were happening on a daily basis. All kinds of situations occurred that were unnatural to a human being, biologically unnatural, so that some things that happened were not registered and not recounted, and others could be told in much greater detail because it was an absolutely unnatural state of affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I'm looking at the text of that interview, which is about eight single-spaced pages, and it begins with this sentence: "The witness is giving this statement voluntarily, and he would describe everything he knows to the best of his knowledge." Is that a correct statement?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Yes. Let me just point out that before this gentleman wrote down what we were saying, we sort of -- not elaborated, but I did speak in greater detail about certain things, so that the man later on decided to record that.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: A moment ago, I asked you about the shooting of Nasic, and you agree that it was a dramatic event and something that a person would never forget. In 1998 you never mentioned the Nasic shooting, did you?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: You probably noticed in my previous statement -- in what I just said, that it was an unnatural situation. And there are many other things that should be told that the public is not aware of or insufficiently aware of, and my statement was such that the gentleman interviewing me had some other obligation and they had to leave. They were limited in time, and I too had things to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. O'Sullivan. I apologise for interrupting you. I too have a question for the witness. Witness, do you remember if during your first statement, which was made spontaneously, without any recording, do you remember whether you spoke about that incident or not?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: I don't remember speaking about it, but I wish to point out that the team or, rather, the gentleman who was conducting the interview was invited, or was asked, to go back to the Tribunal. So we interrupted the interview, and maybe that was the reason why this was not referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you, Mr. O'Sullivan. You may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Could you tell us how you could possibly fail to mention what you describe as a dramatic event, that a person who saw it could never forget?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. O'Sullivan, the witness has already answered that question. Go on to your next question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: [not audible].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. He said that the interviewer was called back to the Tribunal. He had to return immediately, and that they were limited in time so that he was not able to recount everything that he could have recounted. Please don't insist on that and go on to your next question, Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Sir, the reason you did not mention this in 1998, is because you did not witness it, did you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. O'Sullivan. Excuse me. That will not do. Mr. O'Sullivan, you cannot make conclusions that the witness didn't tell about it because he did not witness it. Those are conclusions. You're placing words in the witness' mouth, something that he hasn't said. So please be careful. Continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: With respect, Your Honour, that's cross-examination. You can ask leading questions on cross-examination, in my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I know. Mr. O'Sullivan, there is no need to remind me that we are at cross-examination. But you have asked the question by saying, "The fact that you didn't mention it," is because the witness didn't witness it. It is not what the witness said, it is what you are saying. Otherwise, we're going to go back to that whole discussion about leading or not leading the witness. You were there today, and you saw when I intervened to prevent leading questions. Now, Mr. O'Sullivan, with all due respect, I must say that this is a leading question. The witness has already answered why he didn't speak about it. Why are you insisting on making the witness say that he didn't speak about it because he wasn't there? I'm sorry. I'm not going to let this pass, Mr. O'Sullivan. Either you rephrase the question or I do not allow you to insist on it. So please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Is Your Honour's ruling that we cannot put leading questions to the witness during cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm giving you an orientation for you to be able to continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: On the 11th of July this year, you met again with the Prosecution, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: On that occasion, you said a guard named Stole collected money and returned it to you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I said in the statement that it was a guard whose name was Stole.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And on September 7th of this year, you met with the Prosecution, correct?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: On that occasion you changed your story and said that the guard's name was Jokic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Jokic. Yes. Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Sir, it's incorrect that you witnessed the shooting of Nasic, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: That is not correct. I did see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Someone told you about it after your statement in 1998, correct?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: No, it is not correct. I was present when this cruel murder took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Sir, can you describe the colours of a military uniform of the sort you saw while you were in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: You mean in general terms or somebody in particular, what he wore?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: A military uniform.

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: From time to time, various missionaries would appear in the camp wearing single-coloured uniforms, then representatives of the civilian authorities would appear and guards who were there. That is, the personnel providing security. Among others, there were police uniforms in one colour, then there were camouflage police uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Perhaps I didn't make myself understood. What colour were military uniforms?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Military uniforms were in camouflage colours, and then olive-grey uniforms. There were guards wearing single-coloured olive-grey uniforms. Some guards wore summer military uniforms, others wore winter military uniforms. Some guards, like one of them, for instance, wore a yellow suit, military uniform, with a top and bottom to match. Then there were guards in full police uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Sir, you met with the Prosecutor on July 25th this year, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly whether it was the 25th.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Does that sound about right? Around that date?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: I don't remember. I just didn't recollect that.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: It was late July this year.

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: It could be. Please don't take my word for it. Yes. I apologise. I apologise. It was before the weekend. Today is the 12th. So it was prior to the previous weekend, or this weekend.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Perhaps the Prosecution can confirm that they met with this witness on July 25th and provided us with a proffer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The Prosecution can confirm that a proffer dated 25th July was provided to the Defence. From the transcript, however, Your Honour, I'm not sure whether this witness is following Mr. O'Sullivan's question, because he seems to be referring to this past weekend and relating it to a question about July. So perhaps Mr. O'Sullivan could clear that up.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just want to establish that indeed, as the Prosecutor has said, a proffer was given to us on July 25th or dated July 25th. That's the important point. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Continue, Mr. O'Sullivan, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: When you spoke to the Prosecution on that occasion, you said that the man you knew as Kos wore a military uniform; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: If you understood my description of Kos, I said that Kos occasionally but mostly --

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: In your statement on the 25th of July, dated 25th July, 2000, it says that you said that Kos wore a military uniform. Did you say that then?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Sir, Kos wore a vest or a top without sleeves in military camouflage colours. I'm talking about the top, not about the bottom. In my statement now, I said that on one occasion Kos wore jeans.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Why did you describe him differently on July 25th?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: That's not true. I said that he wore the top part of a uniform without sleeves. It may be a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: You said the person who took your statement --

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Or maybe your intention. No. That is not what I'm saying. I'm telling you about the state of affairs as it was. I said that it was a military uniform or, rather, a jacket without sleeves. A camouflage jacket, that that is what he was wearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And this person you knew as Kos, you're saying that he wore black gloves with the fingers cut off.

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Yes, correct. I noticed that at least on one occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. O'Sullivan. So now it is Mr. Krstan Simic's turn. You have the floor, Mr. Krstan Simic. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Mr. Masan, as you have heard, my name is Krstan Simic, and together with Mr. Lukic, we represent the Defence of Mr. Kvocka. I have a few brief questions for you linked to your testimony today. When testifying, you said that you saw a guard addressing Mr. Kvocka informally with the words boss or chief; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: You said that they had a conversation. Did you hear what they said?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Thank you. You also described the police uniform worn by Mr. Kvocka. Was he always dressed formally in a uniform, according to the rules?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: What was the difference?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: I don't know whether I said that in my statement, but on one occasion when Kvocka came to the camp, he was wearing sneakers, a black T-shirt, also gloves without fingers, and out of a grey Mercedes, he took out a rifle known as a Pumperica, pump-action rifle. Then he was not in uniform. But in most case he came in uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Was he on duty then when he came or did he come for some other reason?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: I don't know whether he was on duty or not, but let me just mention that Kvocka's duty hours, working hours, lasted from the morning till the evening, so that throughout the day Kvocka could be seen within the compound and in the rooms.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: So he was not on duty at night?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: I couldn't see him because I was unable to actually see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Did Mr. Kvocka and Mr. Meakic wear the same military uniforms or, rather, police uniforms?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: I didn't see any difference between the camouflage uniforms. I didn't notice a difference. It was a police uniform. There may have been a difference in shade of colour, but both wore camouflage police uniforms. I didn't notice any difference in the camouflage uniforms worn by one and the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: When was that uniform introduced?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Blue police uniforms. What is the basic colour of that uniform?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: It is blue. I'm sorry. All I know is what I have said.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: How often did you see Mr. Meakic?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: On a daily basis while I was there. I can't tell you I saw him on Mondays and not on Tuesdays, but I did see him every day when he came to the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Because of certain errors in the transcript, that is why I'm asking you these questions, so as to avoid any confusion. You said that sometimes Mr. Meakic and Mr. Kvocka would welcome the investigators in an informal manner. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: I'm not saying that they did this together. If you want me to talk about the ceremony --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me. Mr. Saxon?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I believe the witness used the term ceremony or ceremonious. I don't believe the witness's testimony included the word informal, Your Honour. I just wanted the record to be clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In any event, I think the witness is going to clear up this point. So, Mr. Krstan Simic, continue, please. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Let us clear this point up. Was it a ceremonial, formal, festive welcome or a non-ceremonial one?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Let me tell you, let us see what is a ceremony. A formal line-up, the hoisting of the flag, that, in my mind, is a ceremony. In my understanding, this was not ceremonial. Let me finish, please. What would happen is that they would wait for them, and when the commission appeared, the interrogators who did the interrogations and took notes, he would wait for them at the gate. He would exchange greetings with them. And on one case, he would follow them inside. And this didn't happen once but on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: You said that they did this separately. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: I am speaking about instances.

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: I'm not saying this one did it five times and this one did it five times. I'm saying that one and the other did it at least once.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: But let me ask you, you saw this situation once or twice in the case of Mr. Kvocka; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Yes. He may have done it several times, by only saw him as many times as I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: During those encounters, did you have a feeling or were you able to notice that Meakic was servile in relation to the investigators? What kind of attitude did he have in relation to them? Who was the more important?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: I think any judgement is a personal one, but I think they sort of welcomed these people in the capacity of some sort of hosts. I think that is clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to see Mr. Meakic issuing orders to any individual investigator?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: What about Mr. Kvocka?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Did you have any contact with the police, police investigations? Are you familiar with the organisation of the police?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Before the war in 1992.

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the regulations concerning police security?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the organisation and the structure of the police itself?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. I will finish with the incident that you spoke about. Sorry. Before I do that, let me ask this: You mentioned Mr. Meakic several times?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Yes, I did, several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: You mentioned some uniforms. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] I should like the witness to be shown D38 -- I'm sorry, 38/1 -- 33/71. I apologise. 3/81. 81. That's okay now.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Mr. Masan, in front of you is a photograph showing four individuals. Is that the kind of police uniform that you talked about or is it a military camouflage uniform?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: This is a military camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: So Mr. Kvocka had the same kind of uniform except that the background was blue?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: And so did Mr. Meakic?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Do you know the individuals in the photograph?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: The first man here with his hand raised, this one here, I think that it is a certain Mr. Simo Drljaca. This one here resembles somewhat Zeljko Meakic, but I'm not sure. There are other photographs that I had an opportunity to see with the profile shown, and from the profile you could tell that it was Zeljko Meakic. Here it's very difficult to tell. This third individual here, I believe was a journalist from the Prijedor radio, but he's in the shade.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: For me, it is the fourth individual, but will you have a look at the third one, the one behind the one you think might be Zeljko Meakic?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: It's very hard for me to identify these people in the photograph, but they are all wearing a military kind of uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: I think so. I think that they are all olive-grey in colour. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic, we always have to come back to the same question, to the same problem. If I understand correctly, the witness has not recognised the individual as being Zeljko Meakic. He said that he might be Zeljko Meakic. But you asked the question, "Who is the individual who is behind Zeljko Meakic?" So it seems to me like a conclusion. See how these things turn out to be? MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] No, I'm sorry. I apologise Your Honour. I said the person you think might be Zeljko Meakic. I don't know what's in the transcript. I didn't follow it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I apologise. I'm sorry. I didn't see the transcript.

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: I apologise, but I have to say that if you had the profile of Zeljko Meakic, I can tell you exactly that it is him. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Thank you very much Witness. You told my colleague, Mr. O'Sullivan, about the incident involving Mehmedalija Sarajlic. You said that you had seen the incident?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: There seems to be a mistake in the transcript. Let me repeat my question. You were present during the incident in which Mehmedalija Nasic was killed.

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: At what time of the day did that incident occur?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: It didn't happen during the day, but during the night.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: At what time?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you the exact time. We didn't have any watches on. If you have listened to me, I have spoken about the situation and the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. kind of atmosphere in which we were at that time. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] I should like the usher to show Mr. Masan this photograph so that we can clarify something. This should be our Exhibit 33.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Excuse me. What is going to be the number of the exhibit, Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Registrar, do you already have a copy of this photograph? Because Mr. Simic we need copies of this photograph. We need copies for our own purposes, for our notes. You have to bear that in mind when you present a document. You always have to have a sufficient number of copies of that document. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] I accept your comment, Your Honour, but we have some difficulties regarding the copying machine. We have received the documents from the Prosecutor, and we'll do our best to rectify this problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether you're going to ask the witness to write something on the photograph or not, but go on. We'll see. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Witness, there is a photograph in front of you. Could you mark on that photograph the spot, the location, where the guard Pavlic stood?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Could you locate, could you identify the position of the guard Pavlic before this unfortunate shooting incident?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: No, I cannot, because on this photograph you cannot see the location.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. My question for you is the following: Did you see Mr. Pavlic well?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Yes. I saw him on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: No. I'm referring to that particular incident?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Yes. I saw him during the indent, before the incident, and after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Mr. Masan, we're talking about the incident itself. I would like to know whether he was alone during the shooting?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: There were several guards there, but he was the only one who opened fire. In his immediate vicinity there were several guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: I'm interested about Mr. Pavlic's conduct and his movements before this -- Mr. Nasic's movements before this incident.

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: A group of guards was beating a man outside, who was sitting on a bench. There were between 500 and 600 detainees in the restaurant at that moment, and people were crammed next to each other. He was forced to sleep on the table. When he saw what was going on, he said, "Don't do this. Don't do this." And the order coming from the guards was not to raise our heads. Do you want me to quote any of the guards?

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Let me first ask you a question, Witness. You told us that Mr. Nasic had jumped up from where he was lying down. How did he address the guards?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Let me tell you, sir. It's very difficult for 500 people to be lying down in such a cramped space. I don't know exactly how he did it, but he said, "Please don't do that. Don't do that."

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: You told us he was sleeping on the table.

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: So he was actually laying down on the table. He was sleeping on the table.

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Sir, if you take into account that the room was about 150 metres large and that 500 or 600 people slept in it, could you really talk about lying or sleeping?

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Mr. Masan, you saw Mr. Nasic during the shooting incident.

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Yes, at the moment he erected, when he said, "Don't do that."

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Was he still lying down when he spoke those words?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: I don't know whether he was sitting down or lying down. Do you want me to describe the incident or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic, I am really sorry I have to interrupt you again, but I think that you are forgetting that we are here, that we are present in the courtroom, that there are interpreters working between us. You know that you cannot ask your questions and answer your questions at the same time. The interpreters are having trouble following you. And the reason why you are here is because you have something to tell us and because we have to hear you. Please bear that in mind. Otherwise, I will have to ask Mr. Lukic to remind you every time that you have to slow down. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Mr. Masan, I have to ask you to answer my questions. I need certain answers from you. I don't need any elaboration on those answers. Let me go back to the question that was asked of you by Mr. O'Sullivan. Did you actually see that incident?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. It happened in my vicinity.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Very well then. You saw the incident. How far were you from Mr. Nasic?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: The same as from you at this point. Maybe 4 or 5 metres away from him.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: You told us that Mr. Nasic as asleep. Did you actually see him sleep? What exactly do you mean by "sleep"?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: I'm talking about 500 or 600 people detained in one and the same room.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Yes. But I want you to tell me whether he was asleep or not.

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't see everyone to do everything. It's very difficult for me to tell you. I have to repeat that there were 500 or 600 people in one and the same room. They were cramped. It was like a matchbox. And an order came for us to lie down, and people would lie down on top of one another. And I had an opportunity to see. I was also in danger like himself and other people who were above. People used to sleep on top of one another, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Mr. Masan, I'm trying to establish these very important details with you.

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Before the shooting, did you see Mr. Nasic?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: I saw him react when he said -- let me tell you. What was going on outside was actually interesting for all of us who happened to be detained in the kitchen, in the restaurant at that time. And I saw him react. I saw him get up. And the reason why he was killed was because he had got up.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Did he move towards the guards?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: No, he did not. He was very far away from them. He didn't do anything that would have to bother them.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Do you know the name of any of the guards who were together in the same group with Mr. Pavlic?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: No, I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Regarding this incident, was there any reaction coming from Mr. Meakic, and if so, what kind?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: No, I didn't notice any kind of response. He acted the same way he did during all other incidents or executions, which were a daily occurrence. There was no reaction whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Did you see Mr. Meakic on the following morning or the following day or that night?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: No, I can't remember. I don't know remember whether I saw him on that evening or on the following morning. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: What happened to the injured people? Were they treated or given help in any way and how?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: At that moment, we were again told to lie down, to bends our heads down, and things like that. After awhile, whether it was five days later, ten days later, a week later, I don't know, I had contact with those people. They had been taken somewhere, and they had bandages on their body in the area of the stomach, because that is where they sustained their injuries. But I didn't inquire to find out who it was who had given them help, because of the circumstances, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Were they taken on the very same evening to be given help?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: No, I don't know, because after such incidents, the situation was terrible. We would immediately be ordered to lie down. So I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: After the incident in the camp, as regards the changeover of guards, did you see Mr. Pavlic, or was he perhaps absent for awhile after the incident?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: No, I didn't notice his absence. On the contrary. I would see him very often throughout my remaining time in the camp. Yes, I saw Pavlic often.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Masan. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] I have no further questions for the witness. Thank you, Your Honours. I have completed my cross-examination. Since the witness didn't make any marks on the photograph, we are not going to tender the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Simic. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. You may proceed, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Masan, my name is Toma Fila. I'm a lawyer from Belgrade. I will try not to exceed the ten minutes that remain until the end. From the beginning until the end, you were there in the camp, I should like to know whether during the changeover of the guards, would the same guards always relieve the same group of guards?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: I don't know. I mean, the order of shifts was always the same. I don't know whether you want me to say whether the guards would always be the same, that they would relieve the same people on their positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I'm interested in.

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Well, in most of the cases, I'm not saying that it happened always, but in most of the cases, the guards would come to their assigned positions, to the area that they were in charge of.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you think that it was necessary for someone to give them assignments as to their respective positions?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: I believe it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Why would that be necessary if everyone knew what his location was?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Well, from time to time, guards would leave, be absent for a while. A guard had injured himself on one particular occasion, and then he was away for a while. There was another one who was absent for a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes, but when there were no changes, it would not have been necessary?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: I was referring to the situation as it was in most cases. Let me give you an example. There was a machine-gun nest on the roof of the administration building, so that was the reason for the change.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was always someone there?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: You mean at any particular moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: I don't exactly know, but yes, someone was always there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Let me start with the end of your testimony. You mentioned the person by the name of Krivaja, Stanko Krivaja?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Yes, Stanko Krivaja.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you know in which shift he worked?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: I think he was in what's -- Krkan's shift, Mladjo Radic's shift.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You mentioned another person with whom he was calling out the names of prisoners.

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: He was doing so according to a list that he held in his hand.

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And at that point, he used some vulgar language, and he said, "They have forgotten 50 people." My question in relation to that is the following: Were you able to conclude, on the basis of that, that the list had been made elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: You mean concerning what happened on that day?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yeah. I'm referring to the 50 people who were not on the list when this guy said, "They have forgotten about 50 people."

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: My answer will have to be given in detail. Lists were being made on a daily basis. They were made by people who held certain positions in the camp. Sometime earlier than that, the same individual, Stanko Krivaja, was carrying around some kind of lists, and he called out their names. People went out and disappeared.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: No. I'm referring to this particular list. You said that somebody said that they had forgotten 50 people.

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Yes. They said that 50 people were missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: On the basis of that, were you able to conclude that the list had been made elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: I didn't think about where the list had been made. I'm merely talking about the facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So the call-out was carried out by someone who was not a commander?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with the chain of command. I don't know who the commander was and who wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What was Krivaja? Do you happen to know?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Well, his occupation was that of a driver. He drove at the Autotransport company.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: No, I mean there.

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Well, he had a uniform. He had a gun. He could do as he pleased.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Let me now go back to Krkan. You remember him and you have seen him on the photograph.

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was he any different in respect from other guards? I'm referring to his uniform?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Who was different from whom?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I'm referring to Mladjo Radic. You saw him on this photograph. He was carrying a weapon. He had a uniform.

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: There were some people who had the same kind of uniform as Krkan.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What about the weapon?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: I cannot tell you about the weapon.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Counsel's microphone is switched off. We cannot hear counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Fila, could you please switch on your microphone?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Let me move on to the incident involving Krkan. You told us that he had been in the glass area and the stairway.

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was that the same place as shown on the photograph that you saw?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You said that he had been there for awhile. For how long?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: I cannot tell you. He was accompanied by at least one other individual. There were two people in a camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was he an officer or something of that kind?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Maybe an officer, I don't know. They were standing there for a while. It took me about ten seconds to reach the place where I was, and in that brief interval, in that brief period of time I could see that he was there. But we remained in that area until nightfall.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: My question is the following: You're familiar with that area, the glass area and the stairway.

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: While you could observe him, did he move? Of course you couldn't tell when you were not observing, but while you were observing him, did he move? And what is possible for you to -- what was possible for you -- what was possible for him to see from that spot?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: One could see the interior of the dining area and the corridor through which the people would pass. So that would have been in his line of vision.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Were the two rows of guards in that corridor?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: The rows were in the corridor at the entrance to the kitchen and partially outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I'm only interested in his line of vision. Could he see the rows?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Yes, he could. Not only that, he was able to hear what was going on, to tell what the reactions of people were, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: On that day, was it a kind of a military delegation that was visiting the camp?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: From time to time, a delegation would come to the camp, but I didn't notice that on that particular occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was some kind of washing liquid or powder poured down on the floor?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you ever see that kind of liquid being used for washing dishes while you were at the camp?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: Well, the dishes were washed with something. I don't know what it was. I could see chlorine.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: For the record, maybe I was a bit too fast, but you didn't answer my question. When you saw him, every time you saw him he would be standing on the same location?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: I cannot say that it was every time I saw him. I'm referring to a period of time, and I cannot be more precise. I cannot tell you whether it was for half an hour, one hour, or more. He stood there for a while in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Would you see him elsewhere? Did you see him anywhere else except for that location?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: You mean on that day?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: On that day.

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: I don't remember. I remember that particular location I told you about.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you know when it was that it happened? Was it a kind of holiday?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: During your interview with the investigator, you stated that you had not seen Krkan at night-time. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: I said that I had once seen Krkan in the evening, but I wouldn't see him during the night, to be frank.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You told the Prosecutor that you never saw him preventing the guards to do anything. Did you see anything contrary to that? Did you see him order anything to anyone?

utterances.speaker: OMER MESAN
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This concludes my cross-examination, Your Honour. I've kept my promise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Fila. I don't think we can continue at this point. Mr. Jovan Simic, I don't know whether you have questions or not. You probably do. Mr. Simic. Oh, I apologise. Yes, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, for your orientation, we do not have questions for Mr. Masan. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, Mr. Stojanovic, for having forgotten you. Mr. Simic, Jovan Simic, what about you? MR. J. SIMIC: [Interpretation] We don't have questions for the witness either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, with all due respect to the Chamber, I realise the lateness of the hour. However, this witness is absent from his family and from his employment. I have a very few questions on redirect, and I was wondering if could we work a little bit late today so that we could finish with this witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Saxon. We, as you know, are very sensitive about this matter, and Mr. Keegan has also told us that he has an urgent matter to address. We already have engagements for 3.30, but we'll try. Let us try and finish with this witness. But perhaps, Mr. Keegan, we won't be able to hear the information you wish to convey to us. You said that you had something to tell us at the end of work today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I think the Prosecution's submissions on the issue would take five to ten minutes maximum. The Defence objects to the request and then the Judges could, you know, take the issue and decide it and advise us tomorrow rather than --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Perhaps we should leave that. I don't know what the problem is, but perhaps we could leave that question for the beginning of the morning tomorrow, because if we add all this, we risk going on too long, and you know once we open a debate, we never know where it will lead us, and for that, we need time.
